title: Actitudes, sesgos cognitivos y sentimientos ante la desinformación a través de redes sociales / Attitudes, cognitive biases and feelings in the face of misinformation through social media
screen_reason: Survey of 1,350 residents of the Madrid region (18-80 years, fieldwork 2 Feb - 3 Mar 2022, 40dB) reporting the share of respondents who say they receive news they believe to be false (89.2%) and the channels through which they say they receive it (social media 54.8%, WhatsApp/Telegram 29.2%, traditional media 12.5%). These are self-reported exposure shares with a denominator, i.e. RECALL. The cognitive-bias, feeling and credibility results are attitudes, not exposure, and give no rows.

estimates.platform: Any channel (question asked about fake news received through any route)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they receive news they believe to be false (any frequency other than 'never')
estimates.value_raw: 89.2% believe they receive fake news (complement of the 10.8% who answer 'nunca'/never in the frequency item)
estimates.denominator: 1,350 residents of the Comunidad de Madrid aged 18-80 interviewed by 40dB (online for under-60s, telephone for older respondents); sampling error +/-2.67 points at 95% confidence assuming simple random sampling
estimates.definition: respondent gives any answer other than 'never' to 'Con qué frecuencia recibes noticias que crees que son falsas?' ('How often do you receive news you believe to be false?'): daily, weekly (25.9%), monthly (29.9%) or sporadically (19.5%); 10.8% answer never
estimates.misinfo_def: "noticias falsas" / fake news as perceived by the respondent - the study measures "el comportamiento de los usuarios cuando reciben una noticia que creen que es falsa" ("users' behaviour when they receive news they believe to be false"); no external verification
estimates.source_quote:
Among the conclusions, it should be noted that 89.2% believe

social media, mainly Facebook.
estimates.page_loc: English abstract, p. 467 (also Discussion section 4, p. 472, and Results section 3.1 frequency breakdown)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Entirely respondent-judged ('noticias que crees que son falsas' - news you believe to be false); no external fact-check or coder verification of any item. Survey administered by the polling firm 40dB within a project on digital vulnerability; 74 questions overall.
estimates.moderator_quote:
A survey was
conducted (n=1350), among individuals between 18 and 80 years old, on attitudes, feelings and cognitive
biases operating in disinformation processes.
estimates.notes: Headline exposure figure. The Spanish Results section states the same distribution as '8 de cada 10 ciudadanos declaran recibir noticias que creen que son falsas: el 29,9 % de manera mensual y el 25,9 % de manera semanal; un 19,5 % ... de forma esporádica, y un 10,8 % nunca' ('8 in 10 citizens declare receiving news they believe to be false: 29.9% monthly, 25.9% weekly, 19.5% sporadically, 10.8% never'); the 89.2% is the figure the authors themselves report in the abstract and discussion. Fieldwork was confined to the Madrid region; the authors argue on INE grounds that it extrapolates to other Spanish regions not affected by rural depopulation - a coverage limitation an adjudicator should note.

estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL: the paper is internally inconsistent about the denominator. Results says '(54,8 %) de los encuestados' (of respondents); the Discussion says 'el 89,2 % de los encuestados afirma recibirlas, y de estos, el 54,8 % por redes sociales' ('of these, 54.8% via social media') and the English abstract gives '54% of them'. I recorded the Results wording (share of all 1,350) but an adjudicator may prefer the base of fake-news receivers. missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (a) The frequency bands (29.9% monthly, 25.9% weekly, 19.5% sporadically, 10.8% never) - single bands rather than a cumulative 'at least weekly' threshold, and their complement is already captured by the 89.2% row; the daily band is not printed. (b) Which network within social media (Facebook 54%, Instagram 18%, Twitter 17%) - these are shares of the subset who said social media are a route for fake news, answering which network moves the most, so the denominator is a nested attribution base rather than an exposure denominator. (c) Perceived source of fake news (profiles followed 40.8%, friends 31.2%, colleagues 17%, family 11.1%) - attribution of origin, not an exposure share. (d) Reasons for sharing (41.4% thought it was true, 23% agreed with the content, 19.5% trusted the sender, 10.1% because it spoke badly of an opposing party) - a within-sharers breakdown; the paper never states what share of the whole sample ever shared a false story, so no RECALL/sharing row could be made. The only sharing-related sample share printed is a subgroup one (7.5% among 18-24 year-olds). (e) Behaviour on receiving fake news (36% do nothing, 34.1% try to verify) - behaviour, not exposure. (f) Feelings (worry 66.8%, anger 61%, feeling deceived 58.5%, reinforces my thinking 38.1%, amusing 30%, surprise 27.1%, fear 18.6%) - attitudes. (g) Credibility of the news received (53.7% 'sufficient', 26.2% 'quite', 3.1% 'a lot', summed by the authors to 83%) - a belief/credibility measure and a cross-category sum. (h) All age/education/gender subgroup breakdowns, per the rule to keep the main figure. (i) Figures quoted from the Digital News Report and Edelman (e.g. 56% news consumption via social media, 40% distrust) - cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional survey run by the polling firm 40dB for a research project on digital vulnerability: 1,350 interviews between 02/02/2022 and 03/03/2022 with people aged 18-80, online for respondents under 60 and by telephone for older ones, restricted to the Comunidad de Madrid; stated sampling error +/-2.67 points at 95% confidence assuming simple random sampling; no response rate reported. Exposure is entirely self-reported and self-adjudicated ('news you believe to be false'), with no external verification of any item; the questionnaire had 74 questions and the analysed items are listed in the methods. Regional restriction limits generalisability to Spain as a whole; the denominator of the channel questions is described inconsistently across abstract, results and discussion.
